title: Part 2 of 4: Ethernet CRCs and FCSs in industrial protocols
summary: In this four-part article series, we cover the fundamentals and new innovations related to EtherCAT. In this installment, we detail how EtherCAT detects errors with cyclic redundancy checks, frame che
points: We close with the IEC and ISO standards and the EtherCAT Technology Group or ETG that govern the protocol.

Cyclic redundancy checks or CRCs are the mathematical algorithm used to detect errors in data transmission yielding a frame check sequence or FCS — a 4-byte field at the end of a frame that carries the CRC result.
The FCS on the outer Ethernet frame is separate and independent check covering the entire frame.

summary: In this four-part article series, we cover the fundamentals and new innovations related to EtherCAT. In this installment, we detail how EtherCAT emerged at Hannover Messe 2003 as a hybrid of Lightbus
points: We also explain the on-the-fly frame processing and dedicated EtherType that give EtherCAT its performance edge.
EtherCAT is a control automation technology that has become an open IEC standard around the globe for realtime industrial Ethernet communications.
Speeds evolved from 10 to 100 Mbps and then to Gigabit Ethernet and now beyond.

title: Part 3 of 4: EtherCAT’s stable versioning
summary: In this four-part article series, we cover the fundamentals and new innovations related to EtherCAT. In this installment, we detail the stable versioning that keeps 2004-era EtherCAT devices compatibl

In contrast, the ETG has never needed to change the basic EtherCAT protocol … and has only expanded it into the Automation Protocol or EAP (for control-to-control communication) and EtherCAT G for 1 Gbit/sec and 10 Gbit/sec speeds.
So, a new device today can work on a network from 2004 … even a 100-Mbit/sec device on an EtherCAT G installation.
